title: Modeh Ani
hookLine: the first words on waking thank God for returning the soul

lines: THE FIRST THING IN YOUR HEAD.
cards: What's the first thing you do when you wake up? Be honest. For a lot of people, the hand is on the phone before the eyes are fully open.
Headlines, messages, the weather, somebody's vacation photos. The first thing that gets into your head decides a lot about the next hour.

In Jewish tradition, something is meant to come first: before your feet touch the floor, before you wash, before you check anything. It's twelve Hebrew words long, and children learn it when they're tiny.

teach.b: Modeh ani means I thank, or I acknowledge; a woman says modah ani.
In a plain English rendering, the whole line goes: I thank you, living and everlasting King, for you have returned my soul to me with compassion; great is your faithfulness. Returned my soul.
There's an old Jewish idea that sleep is a little like death, and that each night the soul is entrusted to God, the way you'd leave a coat at a coat check. In the morning you get it back.

And the thanks isn't only for being alive. It's for getting it back with compassion, when maybe you didn't feel you'd earned another day. The last words come from the book of Lamentations, a book of grief.
In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, the verse says of God's mercies: "They are new every morning; great is Thy faithfulness." A line written in the ruins, about new mornings.

teach.h: NO NAME OF GOD, SO SAY IT IN BED.
teach.b: Here's a detail people love: Modeh Ani uses none of the names of God. That's on purpose. It can be said before you've washed your hands, lying in bed, half asleep, even in the dark.
You don't have to be ready to say it.
And it's young, as prayers go: it first appears in a book from the sixteenth or seventeenth century, though the idea behind it is much older.
Many parents say it with small children every morning, sometimes with a little tune. A whole philosophy in twelve words: before you want anything from the day, notice that you got the day.

how: Many Jews say Modeh Ani immediately on waking, still in bed, before washing their hands or saying any other prayer; children often learn it with a simple tune.

o: a blessing said over the first meal of the morning
a thank-you note written to a teacher
I thank you, said on waking for a returned soul

games.q: what's inside the twelve words — tap the pairs.

s: Modeh Ani contains the name of God
it deliberately doesn't, so it can be said in bed before washing.
its last words come from the book of Lamentations
"They are new every morning; great is Thy faithfulness."
Modeh Ani is one of the oldest prayers in the Bible

games.q: you've just woken up. you haven't washed, you're half asleep, and the phone is buzzing. when does Modeh Ani get said?
games.why: right away, in bed: it has no name of God, so it can come first, before anything else.

practice: Imagine you've just woken up: the phone is there, but not yet, and you feel the bed under you and notice you're breathing, here again.

If you pray, say the twelve words, or just modeh ani; if you don't, say a simple thank you, to whoever or whatever you like, for the day you got. Then, and only then, picture your feet touching the floor.

wordCard.voice: Modeh Ani. I thank you: the first words on waking, thanking God for returning the soul with compassion.

orig.note: Hebrew: I thank, I acknowledge. a woman says modah ani.

carryVoice: Your line: thank you, first. Before the phone, before the floor. That's day one hundred nine.
